c01.display: Welcome back to NLP, Simply Explained. This is unit 4, lesson 1: word vectors.
c01.spoken: Welcome back to N L P, Simply Explained. This is unit 4, lesson 1: word vectors.

c02.display: So far, a word has just been a token with an ID number. Today we give each word something richer: a place on a map of meaning.
c02.spoken: So far, a word has just been a token with an ID number. Today we give each word something richer: a place on a map of meaning.

c03.display: This lesson rests on one old idea, from the linguist J. R. Firth in 1957. You shall know a word by the company it keeps.
c03.spoken: This lesson rests on one old idea, from the linguist J. R. Firth in 1957. You shall know a word by the company it keeps.

c04.display: A word vector is a list of numbers that places a word somewhere in a space of meaning. Words with similar meanings end up close together.
c04.spoken: A word vector is a list of numbers that places a word somewhere in a space of meaning. Words with similar meanings end up close together.

c05.display: For example, the word rain might become a list of a few hundred numbers. On their own, the numbers mean little. What matters is where they put the word.
c05.spoken: For example, the word rain might become a list of a few hundred numbers. On their own, the numbers mean little. What matters is where they put the word.

c06.display: Think of a map. Two towns that are close together usually share a lot: weather, food, accent. Word vectors do the same for words.
c06.spoken: Think of a map. Two towns that are close together usually share a lot: weather, food, accent. Word vectors do the same for words.

c07.display: The simplest way to build these vectors is to count. For each word, we count which other words appear near it in lots of text. Here's a tiny made-up example.
c07.spoken: The simplest way to build these vectors is to count. For each word, we count which other words appear near it in lots of text. Here's a tiny made-up example.

c08.display: Rain often appears near wet and cloud, and never near bark.
c08.spoken: Rain often appears near wet and cloud, and never near bark.

c09.display: Storm looks almost the same: wet, cloud, no bark. So the rows for rain and storm are similar, and that similarity is the meaning we're after.
c09.spoken: Storm looks almost the same: wet, cloud, no bark. So the rows for rain and storm are similar, and that similarity is the meaning we're after.

c10.display: Dog is different. It appears near bark, and hardly ever near cloud.
c10.spoken: Dog is different. It appears near bark, and hardly ever near cloud.

c11.display: Real tables are huge, with tens of thousands of columns. So we build vectors in three steps.
c11.spoken: Real tables are huge, with tens of thousands of columns. So we build vectors in three steps.

c12.display: Count: go through millions of sentences, and count the neighbours of every word.
c12.spoken: Count: go through millions of sentences, and count the neighbours of every word.

c13.display: Compress: squeeze the giant table down to a few hundred numbers per word, keeping only the main patterns. A classic way to do this is called singular value decomposition, or SVD.
c13.spoken: Compress: squeeze the giant table down to a few hundred numbers per word, keeping only the main patterns. A classic way to do this is called singular value decomposition, or SVD.

c14.display: Compare: now, to see how similar two words are, we check how close their vectors are.
c14.spoken: Compare: now, to see how similar two words are, we check how close their vectors are.

c15.display: Here are some illustrative similarity scores, from zero for unrelated up to one for very similar.
c15.spoken: Here are some illustrative similarity scores, from zero for unrelated up to one for very similar.

c16.display: Storm is very close to rain.
c16.spoken: Storm is very close to rain.

c17.display: Umbrella is fairly close: it shows up in many of the same sentences.
c17.spoken: Umbrella is fairly close: it shows up in many of the same sentences.

c18.display: And banana is far away. They simply don't keep the same company.
c18.spoken: And banana is far away. They simply don't keep the same company.

c19.display: Something surprising happens in a good vector space: directions carry meaning, so you can do maths with words.
c19.spoken: Something surprising happens in a good vector space: directions carry meaning, so you can do maths with words.

c20.display: Start at king, take away man, add woman, and the nearest word is queen.
c20.spoken: Start at king, take away man, add woman, and the nearest word is queen.

c21.display: Start at Paris, take away France, add Italy, and you land near Rome. The direction from a country to its capital is roughly the same everywhere.
c21.spoken: Start at Paris, take away France, add Italy, and you land near Rome. The direction from a country to its capital is roughly the same everywhere.

c22.display: It even works for grammar: walked minus walk plus swim lands near swam.
c22.spoken: It even works for grammar: walked minus walk plus swim lands near swam.

c23.display: Why is this such a big deal? Compare it with what we had before.
c23.spoken: Why is this such a big deal? Compare it with what we had before.

c24.display: With one ID per word, every word is equally far from every other. To the model, rain is as close to storm as it is to banana.
c24.spoken: With one ID per word, every word is equally far from every other. To the model, rain is as close to storm as it is to banana.

c25.display: With word vectors, similar words sit close together, and the model can use that. Anything it learns about storm partly carries over to rain.
c25.spoken: With word vectors, similar words sit close together, and the model can use that. Anything it learns about storm partly carries over to rain.

c26.display: Time for a quick quiz. Which word's vector is probably closest to the vector for rain: storm, banana, or Tuesday?
c26.spoken: Time for a quick quiz. Which word's vector is probably closest to the vector for rain: storm, banana, or Tuesday?

c28.display: It's storm. Rain and storm appear near the same words, like wet, cloud and weather, so their vectors end up close together.
c28.spoken: It's storm. Rain and storm appear near the same words, like wet, cloud and weather, so their vectors end up close together.

c29.display: Let's recap. A word gets its meaning from the company it keeps.
c29.spoken: Let's recap. A word gets its meaning from the company it keeps.

c30.display: A word vector is a list of numbers that places the word on a map of meaning.
c30.spoken: A word vector is a list of numbers that places the word on a map of meaning.

c31.display: Words with close vectors have similar meanings.
c31.spoken: Words with close vectors have similar meanings.

c32.display: And directions in that map carry meaning, so king minus man plus woman lands near queen.
c32.spoken: And directions in that map carry meaning, so king minus man plus woman lands near queen.

c33.spoken: Next lesson: Word2Vec. How does a computer learn word vectors just by reading?
